content: Repetitive low-frequency transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been hypothesized to suppress activity in the undamaged contralesional motor cortex, while high-frequency rTMS has been proposed to enhance excitability in the damaged hemisphere's motor cortex. These mechanisms are thought to potentially aid in functional recovery following a stroke. The objective of this study was to evaluate both the efficacy and safety of rTMS in improving functional outcomes for individuals who have experienced a stroke. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Stroke Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, up to May 2012. Additional searches were performed in Chinese databases, ongoing trial registries, and relevant reference lists. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing rTMS therapy to either sham therapy or no therapy were included, while studies reporting only laboratory parameters were excluded. Two independent reviewers selected eligible trials, assessed their quality, and extracted data. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion. A total of 19 trials, involving 588 participants, were included in the review. Two trials, comprising 183 participants, demonstrated no significant improvement in the Barthel Index score following rTMS treatment (mean difference [MD] 15.92, 95% confidence interval [CI] -2.11 to 33.95). Similarly, four trials with 73 participants showed no statistically significant effect of rTMS on motor function (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.51, 95% CI -0.99 to 2.01). Subgroup analyses based on stimulation frequency or duration of illness also failed to reveal any significant differences. Adverse events associated with rTMS were generally mild. The most commonly reported side effects included transient or mild headaches (2.4%, 8 out of 327 participants) and localized discomfort at the stimulation site. The authors concluded that current evidence does not support the routine use of rTMS for stroke rehabilitation. Further research, involving larger sample sizes, is necessary to establish an optimal rTMS protocol and to evaluate its long-term effects on functional recovery.
